rounds.title: The login form
rounds.context: This code checks a username and password at login. It glues what the user typed straight into the SQL text.
rounds.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND password_hash = '" + hash + "'";
const user = await db.get(sql);
rounds.why: Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL command itself. A quote character in the input can end the string early and change what the query means. That's SQL injection.
tests: alex with the right password logs in
O'Brien (a real name with an apostrophe) can log in
' OR '1'='1 typed as the name must NOT log anyone in

options.feedback: A parameterized query sends the SQL and the values separately. The database always treats the values as plain data, so no input can change the command.

options.code:
const safeName = name.replace("'", "");
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + safeName + "' AND password_hash = '" + hash + "'";
options.feedback: Stripping characters breaks real names like O'Brien, and replace() here only removes the first quote. Blocklists always miss something.
Hiding error messages is good hygiene, but the query is still built from raw input, so the vulnerability is still there.
Checks in the browser help honest users, but anyone can send a request without your form. Validation must happen on the server, and it still doesn't replace parameters.

rounds.takeaway: Never build SQL by gluing strings together. Use parameterized queries (also called prepared statements) every time.

rounds.title: The search box
rounds.context: A shop's search box finds products whose name contains the search text.
rounds.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
const results = await db.all(sql);
rounds.why: Same problem in a different place: the search text becomes part of the SQL command.
tests: searching children's toys works (it contains an apostrophe)
a search containing quotes and SQL words is treated as plain text

options.feedback: The % wildcards are added to the value, not the SQL. The query text never changes, whatever is typed.

options.code:
if (q.includes("SELECT")) throw new Error("Nice try");
const sql = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
options.feedback: Blocking keywords is a guessing game: lowercase, other keywords or encoded input slip past, and children's toys still breaks.

options.code: const sql = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q.slice(0, 20) + "%'";
options.feedback: Limiting the length makes an attack a bit harder, not impossible. Short inputs can still change the query.

options.code:
const results = (await db.all("SELECT * FROM products"))
  .filter((p) => p.name.includes(q));
options.feedback: This is safe from injection, but it loads every product on every search. Parameterized LIKE is safe and lets the database do the work.

rounds.takeaway: Wildcards, numbers, dates: they all go in as parameters. The SQL text should be the same for every request.

rounds.title: The order page
rounds.context: The order page reads an order number from the address, like /orders?id=1042.
rounds.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = " + req.query.id;
const order = await db.get(sql);
rounds.why: There are no quotes here, so it's even easier: anything after the number becomes more SQL.
tests: an id followed by extra SQL is treated as plain data

options.feedback: Validate that it's really a number, then still pass it as a parameter. Two layers: validation for good errors, parameters for safety.

options.code: const sql = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = '" + req.query.id + "'";
options.feedback: Adding quotes just moves the problem: a quote in the input can still close the string.

options.code: const order = await db.get("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = " + req.query.id + " LIMIT 1");
options.feedback: LIMIT 1 changes how many rows come back, not what the query means. The input is still part of the SQL.

options.code: const order = await db.get("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?", [req.query.id]);
options.feedback: Safe from injection, good. But 1042abc should be rejected with a clear error, not quietly passed to the database. Validate the type too.

rounds.takeaway: Validate input for correctness, and parameterize it for safety. You need both.

rounds.title: Sort by column
rounds.context: A table can be sorted by clicking a column header, which sends ?sort=price or ?sort=name.
rounds.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY " + req.query.sort;
const rows = await db.all(sql);
rounds.why: Parameters work for values, not for column names, so the usual fix doesn't apply here. What's left?
tests: a sort value that isn't a known column is refused

options.feedback: An allowlist maps what the user asks for to SQL you wrote yourself. User input never reaches the query text at all.

options.code: const rows = await db.all("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY ?", [req.query.sort]);
options.feedback: Most databases treat a parameter here as a constant value, so nothing gets sorted. Parameters can't stand in for column names.

options.code:
const sort = req.query.sort.replace(/[^a-z_]/g, "");
const rows = await db.all("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY " + sort);
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but it still lets users pick any column, including ones you never meant to expose. An allowlist is exact.

options.code:
const rows = (await db.all("SELECT * FROM products"))
  .sort((a, b) => (a[req.query.sort] > b[req.query.sort] ? 1 : -1));
options.feedback: No injection, but any property name is accepted, and sorting everything in the app gets slow. An allowlist keeps it explicit.

rounds.takeaway: When something can't be a parameter (column names, sort direction), map the input to an allowlist of values you wrote yourself.
